1) Lichenoid (lichen planus–type) eruption or lichenoid drug reaction — Most likely given violaceous, indurated papules/plaques and occurrence at/around a scar (Koebnerization) in an immunosuppressed transplant recipient; can be subacute, non-tender, and encircle scars.

2) Fixed drug eruption — Fits acute-onset, well-demarcated violaceous plaques that localize to the same site after drug exposure; transplant patient on multiple meds and may have intermittent exposures.

3) Annular granulomatous eruption (granuloma annulare or erythema annulare centrifugum) — Explains annular appearance with central clearing and indurated violaceous papules; often asymptomatic and can appear on the trunk.

4) Dermatophyte infection (tinea corporis, possibly atypical in immunosuppression) — Annular lesion with central clearing and raised border is classic; immunosuppression can alter appearance and lessen pruritus.

5) Scar-related / foreign-body inflammatory reaction or early cutaneous malignancy (squamous cell carcinoma) — Transplant recipients are at higher risk for SCC arising in scars; presentation is less typical but must be considered given location.

Recommended immediate diagnostic actions (to confirm/triage):
- 4-mm punch biopsy of an active lesion for histopathology (H&E) with PAS/GMS fungal stains and consideration of direct immunofluorescence if lichenoid disease suspected.
- KOH scraping of the leading edge for dermatophyte evaluation and fungal culture as indicated.
- CBC with differential (look for neutrophilia/eosinophilia) and tacrolimus trough level.
- Review recent medication exposures (including intermittent antibiotics, NSAIDs, sulfa drugs, topical agents, and over-the-counter pills) and recent topical adhesive use.

Management until results:
- Avoid introducing or stopping immunosuppressants without transplant team input.
- Keep the area clean, avoid topical irritants/adhesives, and do not apply topical steroids or antibiotics until biopsy/KOH if a fungal infection is possible (if strong suspicion of eczema/lichen planus, a short course of topical high-potency steroid could help but best after biopsy).
